stories.titleZh: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
stories.author: Jowsey
summaryZh: Introducing Kimi K3.1 ProWe're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities. We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions. Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API. The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.

Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2%, above K3's 55.95%.

stories.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
stories.titleZh: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
stories.author: ltratt
summaryZh: Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying [W]e should be more ambitious1 with the software we build There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader2, this money overflow bug, etc. This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free3, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed. That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post). As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever. But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use. If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more. Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were: Ripgrep Compiling Rust Syscall and filesystem overhead At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations or building a custom OS or a funny layer that fakes out syscalls would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now. For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up. My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now4. Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed. When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher)5. For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats6. BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle7. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing8. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build. Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, Max Hawkins, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion. I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done. I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that would be a super interesting thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago. Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course): If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do. And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with this (although it can speed up implementation once you have a clean spec), but for that, I was able to set up some kind of janky set of consistency checks between all of the inconsistent explanations of the game rules, which got fairly close to a correct set of rules (approximately as close as what someone else did with much more human effort and less of a systematic approach), which was enough to compare it to someone else's implementation and get a working set of rules. This setup did cost a lot more in tokens than a more manual approach. But it was "only" a month or two of the $200/mo OpenAI subscription with GPT-5.1/5.2, which is a lower cost than the cost in time of me sitting down and writing a clean spec for the game, i.e., a copy of the rules that is actually consistent and correct. I feel like a lot of problems are in something like this class of problem, where it's possible to set up some kind of at least partially self-checking setup that a human can spend a small amount of time on. This also feels analogous to the situation about software testing at large, where (before coding agents) I found fuzzing and property-based testing to be highly effective. For most domains, people told me some kind of reason this kind of testing wouldn't work, but when I've tried these techniques with all of the domains people told me these techniques don't work for, they work fine. They're somewhat more work to apply, but they're still applicable and, AFAICT, more efficient and effective than writing traditional unit tests. Part of the gist of Yossi's comment is that people aren't doing this kind of thing. Considering how many more bugs I see now than I used to, e.g., the last time I opened up the web chat for a big AI lab, I ran into a double-digit number of bugs within one minute, it's hard to say that Yossi is wrong. But, to that point, I still have my original opinion. Just because other people are pumping out vast quantities of barely working slop doesn't mean that you have to do the same thing. Appendix: a few "random" examples The examples in the body of the post I gave for things I've done are tooling things I never would've done. There are a lot more things like that as well since it's so easy to build "works for me" quality tooling that's intended solely for me. I do think it's possible to go further than is productive, e.g., Steve Yegge wrote a lot about Gas Town and how productive it was, but when he was building his next agentic framework, he noted that he never used Gas Town to successfully build anything other than Gas Town and here's someone playing his game that's been created with his next gen framework (the commenter's references to $1B are because Yegge says his game is in the running for being the first solo-run billion dollar company), people were into Ralph Loops for a while even though, when I tried comparing them, they seemed worse than just doing the naive thing I was doing at the time, normal loops with context where you sometimes clear context as appropriate instead of doing it by default at the completely arbitrary point of when a single turn is completed, etc., so I've tried to stick to things where the impact is pretty direct. Besides the obvious reason this has been effective, the dramatic change in model and harness capability over time means that what tooling it makes sense to build changes very quickly, so spending a lot of time working on any particular tool that will be suboptimal at best and quite possibly obsolete in three months doesn't really make sense. And, for a lot of my personal tools, my assumption is that an AI lab will obsolete anything I make in short order. For a very silly example of this, I have a tool that was useful since the release of GPT-5.6 Sol that restarts codex when it finds a memory leak. Presumably, OpenAI will fix this at some point and this tool will become worthless. For a slightly less silly example, take the Rust interpreter I had some agent build. For token-budget reasons, a lot of things that ought to be done for a very high-performance interpreter haven't been done. For example, the interpreter doesn't modify the actual Rust front-end compiler to make it easy to take updates; performance would be much better if I just made changes to the Rust front-end, but I don't have the token budget to maintain a compatible fork of the Rust compiler, but this shouldn't be a problem for OpenAI. OpenAI committed $10B+ on getting access to Cerebras while also preventing Anthropic from having access. Funnily enough, for coding, on many tasks, if you actually use one of their SOTA models and compare it to what you get from Anthropic, the actual speedup isn't all that large because of time spent on things like compiling Rust. Given that they were willing to commit $10B+ on this, it stands to reason that they'll eventually do a better job at speeding up the relevant tools than anyone could feasibly do outside an AI lab, so there's not much point in spending too much effort on this (this could arguably be untrue if non-coding tasks are expected to completely dominate future OpenAI revenue in the short term, but even then, given what they pay for tokens vs. what I pay, it still seems like it would make sense for them to speed a lot of these things up given that I could do it outside of a lab; perhaps there's some kind of argument like, if you have access to their usage data, there are so many more important bottlenecks that this one doesn't make sense to prioritize, but it still seems like it should make sense for them at some point even if it doesn't fall into the top 100 bottlenecks for Cerebras-enabled coding agents). Another kind of thing that one might not call ambitious, but that speaks to the kind of thing that's possible, are games that I've made. There are games I've thought about and wanted to make that I don't think are generally enjoyable enough that they make sense for a real audience, but that I've wanted to play. For example, ever since reading David Gerrold's Star Wolf books in the 90s, I've wanted to play a game that implements combat as described in the books, which is a sort of like submarine combat. At least among realistic war games, this genre is extremely niche because almost everybody finds naval combat boring, and submarine combat is a particularly boring subgenre of naval combat games, so this doesn't really make sense as a money-making game, but it's so easy to implement games that I had an agent implement the game so I could play it for an hour or two. I never would've spent 10-20 hours implementing a game so that I could play it for an hour or two, but I'd spend 5 minutes. I've also previously mentioned implementing a game with the same rules as Scout and Guards of Atlantis 2 and other board games. I was never going to take the time to implement these games by hand just so I have a way to play with my friends on the occasions where we can't get together in-person, but I'm happy to have an LLM bash these things out. And, of course, for people who want to make games with a wider audience, there's a game renaissance going on right now due to coding agents. It's amazing how many interesting and creative games are being made now that having programming skills and the time to put them to use is no longer a bottleneck for making games. Data analysis is another thing where the productivity multiplier can be very high and I can do all sorts of things I never would've done. As I've mentioned in a number of my last posts, I have way too many of these projects to really be able to write them up, even when attempting to write very quickly and bash out posts in half an hour apiece. When I've talked to people about their one-off tooling, there's a lot of fun stuff people have done. For example, here's something Peter Geoghegan mentioned a month or two back: I had Fable implement a custom Neovim Lua function that formats code according to my very specific preferences. This is both something I don't want to maintain myself and inherently a Rube Goldberg device. Theoretically I could accomplish the same outcome in a principled way by patching clang-format, but my requirements are so exact that I think that approach would never be satisfactory. We use a tool call pgindent, which is our fork of bsd_indent. You can approximate the same formatting rules using clang-format, but that isn't good enough. If I commit something that isn't perfectly formatted/indented according to pgindent, I get a CI failure that I'm expected to fix quickly -- something I'd really prefer to avoid ... Practically speaking, getting slick, clang-format-style formatting that avoids nag emails about misindented code requires a total architectural mess (I also don't want to spend the time developing a principled approach, but that's really a separate issue). The function allows me to effortlessly format a given block of code from Neovim, similar to the clang-format LSP integration. I'm being unreasonably fussy here, of course, but I find that LLMs allow me to be this exacting about tooling. The function performs multiple passes: an initial formatting pass using clang-format/clangd, and a separate formatting pass using pgindent. I need it to do both because clang-format handles some cases correctly that pgindent misses. This is brittle because I only want to format the code within a range of lines selected via block visual mode (I don't want to run clang-format on code not added by my patch). This conflicts with pgindent's design; it can only format whole C files. Figuring out which relevant subset of the temp whole file buffer needs to be copied back into my working buffer is nontrivial. The initial line range I selected doesn't directly map to the affected C AST elements. So the function uses tree-sitter to intelligently delineate the exact subset of the temp indented C code that needs to be copied back. The rules need to be fuzzy in exactly the right way for cases where my selection straddles the same block of code. There are a bunch of edge cases. Another complicating factor is that pgindent relies on a typedef file generated with objdump to identify types; without that file, the formatting looks wonky. The formatting function dynamically generates any extra typedefs from clangd, for that one file, so I don't have to worry about a stale typedef file (I might have created a new struct seconds before running the formatting tool, I don't want to run objdump on the whole postgres binary each time, that'd blow up latency). This will probably continue to work, even as further changes are made to our fork of bsd_indent that somewhat alter how code is formatted, which happens from time to time. I'm skeptical of the saaspocalypse. But I do think that LLMs are writing a lot of useful software that would have been insanely uneconomical to write any other way. There's an interesting small subset of software that'd be impossibly tedious for any human to maintain, relative to the value that it creates. I also caught with Malis while writing this and found out about all sorts of fun stuff he's been doing. It's enough that writing it all up in detail could be its own post, but one fun thing is that, the last time I taked to him about pgrust verification, he mentioned using Kani to verify some parts of the code. He's since switched to Lean and has been using Lean to verify things that are too complex to do in Kani. This would be another topic for another post, but I wonder why people have generally settled on Lean for LLM-driven proofs (as opposed to, say, ACL2). I wonder how Lean would look in an updated version of this theorem prover comparison, or if someone were to run a theorem prover eval that's analogous to this language eval. Of course, you can think of plenty of examples out of AI labs, such as a mid-sized team Anthropic building an internal replacement for GitHub as well as some other tooling in five months A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. I think these kinds of examples are interesting and they point to where the industry will be in the not-so-far future, but what you can do with unlimited tokens, while relying on other infrastructure and tooling built with unlimited tokens doesn't tell you much about what you can accomplish today without unlimited funds. Projects like pgrust as well as projects that people I know do in their spare time (of which I've probably mentioned something like 1%—there are just a lot of these, like David Turner creating an skipper for podcasts that's "works for me" quality that works better than anything he could find, the spare-time projects Dennis Snell mentioned here, etc.) are more representative of what you can do today. In this post, we're going to use ambitious in a way that feels consistent to me, but that one could argue is overloaded. I'm using this to mean, doing more than you could've before, in a generic sense. One could say that there's a difference between building a project that's larger than was reasonably feasible before and building some kind of super-specialized tool that could've been done before but just wasn't worth the time to build. comments.author: wfn
comments.textZhHtml:
Think of it like an assert.

Sometimes you do want some flow to terminate if a schema / data contract is breached, and not have this broken data contract propagate elsewhere / outwards.

And/or, it is a perfectly valid pattern to indeed add try..catch, and contain (hence "localize") the issue there and then. If there is a way to handle this breach - you will need some kind of if check anyway. Catching by matching against the particular KeyError exception is in fact robust - and if you forgot to add an intended catch, then the exception will propagate upstack, yes - which is what you want - and this way you do not need to worry about forgetting an "if None" check.

This sort of approach makes it structurally impossible to "forget" - if exception is not caught, it will abort the cannot-be-null breach continuing with program flow, possibly (e.g.) ending up persisted in some place it shouldn't be, causing problems later.

comments.author: secabeen
comments.textZhHtml:
The tech sector is the most software-defined and virtual of all sectors, it's natural that they are first to change. Other industries need to make capital investments to adapt to change.

You can see a similar history with electrification. A few industries went quickly, but then it took like a decade of little growth before the true benefits showed up. As an example, take a factory that was built around hyrdo-power like a grain mill. You can't just take an electric motor and drop it in in place of the water wheel. It doesn't fit, the wheel is outside, there isn't room between the mill and the wall, etc. Only when you completely rebuild a new mill building designed around the features and limitations of the electric motor do you see the major benefits.

Same thing here; it will be new factories and new companies that are designed from the ground up around AI and its benefits and limitations that really move the needle.

comments.author: Zigurd
comments.textZhHtml:
Cool analogy, but there's another possibility: software is uniquely suited for being boosted by LLM-based coding agents. That's not to say LLMs are useless in other domains, but they may not yield as much benefit.

Software creation tools have been worked on for decades to keep fallible human coders out of trouble as much as possible. Starting with compilers that enforce or at least encourage coding style humans can understand. Compilers embody formal definitions of language syntax. Lint and other static analysis technologies contribute by identifying problematic patterns in code. Leak detectors identify memory management problems. Profilers identify performance problems.

Few other endeavors have this much tooling that serendipitously happens to help help LLM-based agents be more useful and less error prone.

A lot of discussion around AI is very high-level and abstract. It helps to dig in and identify the characteristics that actually make a domain more or less amenable to being boosted by AI.

comments.author: eslaught
comments.textZhHtml:
You're missing the biggest suggestion from the GP's post: that the key to LLM success is verifiability.

Software has high verifiability through compilers, linters, static analysis, leak/memory corruption detection tools, or the very least, running the program to see if it crashes.

Math (as has been making the headlines recently) has high verifiability through automated theorem provers. Notably some of the non-mechanized math results from LLMs have been demonstrated to be wrong (and presumably many more are being checked; these aren't exactly easy to understand proofs).

Game playing (chess, go, Star Craft, etc.) is similarly verifiable: you get your score and you always know how you did in the end (even if not in the moment).

Making assumptions about LLMs in non-veriable domains is making a claim about LLMs that doesn't match their current capabilities. Maybe they'll get there and maybe they won't; I can speculate as well as you can but we're both guessing, so I'm not sure how much value the speculation has.

comments.author: brabel
comments.textZhHtml:
First of all , this is an observation of facts in the reality we live in. I agree with the OP argument that these things are intrinsically linked when we just observe the facts without trying to impose our beliefs on them. If we accept that, we can try to theorize about why that may be.
My theory is that people are nice when they live among others who look and behave like themselves because that what humans did for almost their whole existence as a species. Archeological evidence suggests that if you met a stranger, someone not from your tribe, chances were high they would be a danger, not an opportunity to make a new friend. So humans seem to have evolved to not trust outsiders, not just strangers. In a small society, conformity is highly valued because doing things without understanding its consequences could often end up in catastrophe. People didn’t understand the world, and other tribes, well enough to have any confidence in whether a new behavior would be beneficial or not. So we end up with humans who trust and depend on others from their own tribe for everything, are highly distrustful of outsiders, and not looking like yourself is the greatest sign that someone is an outsider, and who value and demand conformity as a matter of survival.
The world of today breaks some of these expectations in some ways, but they are still mostly accurate in my opinion.
People who are more open minded tend to be so because they live in fairly cosmopolitan areas, but those also tend to be bigger cities where you don’t really know most people and where trusting others becomes harder, especially when many people have completely different backgrounds than you.

comments.author: brabel

I think you didn't understand my claim. My claim is simple, my long explanation above was meant for you to arrive at these conclusions yourself:

* people are nice when they still behave in the old, tribal way.

* the tribal way is always going to be creating individuals who are racist and conformant/conservative.

* not behaving the tribal way means going outside the conformist mold, which means you take risks and eventually learn by experience that taking more risks come with consequences. You become less trustful of everyone, while almost paradoxically proclaiming yourself to be more open.

This fits observation. If you believe it's wrong, you must demonstrate why with supporting evidence without contradicting the evidence I've used, obviously.

comments.author: Viliam1234
comments.textZhHtml:
Consider what happens if you have a community that is very nice, very trusting, and open to everyone including complete strangers who behave weirdly.

At the beginning it can be a nice place. Until the first abuser finds them. And then... depends on the abuser.

This is not a theory; I have seen it happen, often in groups of nerds who are somewhat naive about how real life works. Then a new guy comes, borrows some money from each of them individually, then disappears. Or a new guy comes, invites a girl to his place, and rapes her. Sometimes some people even get suspicious about the new guy, but is a taboo to express such thoughts loudly, to spread suspicion in a group based on mutual trust.

To avoid things like this, you need to split people into "those I trust" and "strangers". Different people and cultures draw the line differently. For some of them, "those I trust" only includes people they have known for a few years. It is frustrating for a newcomer, and you often wish you were able to do something so that they accept you faster. Unfortunately, if that worked, the abuser would probably do the same thing.

Another strategy is to have mutual friends vouch for someone. But this only works when it is a part of the culture, where people know that vouching for someone brings heavy consequences if that person turns out to be an abuser. In cultures that do not have such experience, abusers often do the trick where they befriend someone, use them to get introduced to their friends, and while the first target is like "this is a nice stranger that I have met yesterday", their friends are like "this is a nice person recommended by my trusted friend, which means I can trust them too", and then the abuser exploits them. (And when they complain to the first target "why did you make me trust such a horrible person", the first target is confused "well, I actually barely knew them, this was a horrible misunderstanding". But the abuser probably has a lot of experience creating such misunderstandings on purpose.)

Finally, you can have a close community that is very difficult to enter. You can trust everyone in that community, because if they do something bad, they will be kicked out, or worse. But this requires the community to be very difficult to enter, and to have ways to punish the abusers in a way that actually hurts them. (Merely kicking someone out of the community is not enough, if there are hundreds of communities, and the abuser simply infiltrates the next one.)

Abusers exist. You need to build a firewall somewhere. There are different places where you can build it, but you have to build it somewhere, or you get hurt.

comments.author: Dylan16807
comments.textZhHtml:
You're talking about it being hard to join the community.

That's arguably xenophobic depending on how you interpret the word. But it doesn't require anything resembling racism or homophobia.

I'm objecting to the idea that the downside of a tight-knit community is some kind of bigotry. Not just barriers to entry.

(Alternatively, if it's not a specific community, it's some super-wide group based on some obvious feature, than that group isn't keeping out abusers and someone in a different group has probably the same odds of being an abuser.)

If you want to assume you can trust your network, so you don't need security in the hosts, you need to have a sysadmin who secures the network or have it airgapped directly.  You can get rid of all of that, but then you must assume your network is untrusted and need to have security in every service you run.

stories.title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?
stories.titleZh: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?
stories.author: gnabgib
summaryZh: Thanks for reading! If you haven’t subscribed, please click the button below:By subscribing, you’ll join over 80,000 people who read Apricitas!America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone. That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008. Yet there’s no generalized recession today—instead, this period of job loss coincides with the rise of AI systems that can compose wholesale novels, photorealistic images, soundalike music, and practically every other form of digital art, en masse and at extremely low costs. Is this the fall of the Creative Class?Proving the exact amount of AI-driven job loss in the arts is extremely difficult. Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights. The effects of AI are also hard to disentangle from other factors currently affecting arts businesses, like consolidation in Hollywood, offshoring of content production, or the continued displacement of traditional media providers in favor of social media creators. Yet perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.Some of those digital job losses are just a continuation of prior trends, like in the publishing industry where technological change has been continually grinding away newspaper and magazine jobs for decades. Yet for sectors like live broadcasting, streaming, or graphic design, recent experience is an unusual downturn compared to the tranquility of years prior. Then there’s the worst-hit sector, movie & sound recording, which has been bleeding jobs at a nearly unprecedented pace over the last three years.Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total. At the depths touched this summer, total employment was lower than at any point since the 2008 recession and approaching the lowest point in 30 years. The streaming era has proven an extremely difficult transition, with traditional films and TV shows losing watch time to user-generated and increasingly AI-assisted or AI-generated content flows.Overall, nearly half the media job losses of the last four years have been concentrated in the movie & sound recording sector that includes Hollywood. Written publishing has been the next-largest source of job loss, with employment down by more than 70k over the same time frame. Yet the job losses have by no means been contained to any particular part of media; instead they’ve hit nearly every subsector at some point. Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months. Will further AI development continue displacing workers in creative industries?To understand what could happen to the business of art amidst the rise of AI, it’s important to understand what did happen to it during the first digital transition, the rise of the internet.It was the turn of the millennium, and Metallica had a problem. Demos of their upcoming, unreleased tracks were bouncing around radio and the internet, originally leaked onto a new internet file-sharing website called Napster. There they found thousands of files shared amongst hundreds of thousands of users, many of which were direct rips of albums that sold for $15 being offered for free. The most anticipated albums were often leaked online even before they were on store shelves. Metallica sued Napster for copyright infringement, and they were soon joined by separate suits from other prominent artists and eventually the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).Much of the general public was understandably unsympathetic to Metallica, perceived as a bunch of already-successful millionaires trying to bilk even more money from listeners, and were even less sympathetic towards the RIAA, perceived as scurrilous middlemen who take from artists and fans alike. But the two of them easily won their lawsuit, forcing Napster into bankruptcy. Yet Metallica may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.The modern internet made file-sharing extremely easy, and no matter how much whac-a-mole companies played, they could not possibly catch every illegal upload. The perennial threat of piracy undermined their copyright and limited their ability to charge for music. Eventually, the value of individual songs fell to the point that companies like Spotify and Apple Music could swoop in to acquire massive catalogues, consolidate them, and charge a comparatively trivial fee for access. For what a single Metallica album would have cost in 2000, you can now get a month’s worth of unlimited access to nearly all human-made music.The music industry has never returned to the heyday paydays of the peak CD era—even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales. This was a massive boon to consumers, but it was also a squeeze on musicians that forced them to fundamentally change their business model over time. Instead of just selling records to earn money directly, music itself increasingly became a loss-leading advertisement for the live concerts (and merch) that provided a growing share of artists’ income. Tours got longer, venues got bigger, ticket prices skyrocketed, and musicians frequently took on roles closer to public influencers than isolated artistes. Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.Of course, there were still significant downsides to the transition into the streaming era. Bands (especially smaller ones) complain about the unending pressure to always be on tour. Musicians whose content was suited to home listening lost out to those more suited to giant festivals. Even accounting for concert revenues, musicians made less money than before. Yet musicians fared better than many areas of entertainment subsectors because there was a live component to fall back on—for many media industries, the digital era left no such comfort.Over time, the business of video has moved in the opposite direction of music—out of the theatre and into the home. Hollywood formerly made most of its money enticing customers to visit sold-out movie theatres, but these were gradually supplanted by broadcast TV, cable, and physical media. Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval. That is, until the modern streaming era.Today, the plethora of video options and the rise of social media have sent video producers into a vicious competition for limited attention. Even before adjusting for inflation, movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop. The mountain of free user-generated content on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, or social media was already presenting harsh competition for traditional video companies in the years before ChatGPT’s launch, and now streaming services are also competing with a flood of AI-generated content. The business model of video media is fundamentally getting squeezed, and unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.The actual worst-case scenario for creative workers amidst the AI revolution is something similar to what happened to the publishing industry after the advent of the internet—that is, near-total collapse of their fundamental business model. Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping. Magazine publishers likewise have let 66% of their staff go since the 90s, while book publishers have lost 40%.The routine informational updates that previously formed newspapers’ bread-and-butter were all de-bundled—box scores moved to sports websites, stock movements went to financial websites, forecasts went to weather websites—each loss compounding on itself to undermine consumers’ need to buy the paper. Search engines became the first place people looked to for information, and newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead. The collective of social media users became faster at breaking any news story than a daily paper could ever hope to be. When papers eventually did start aggressively paywalling content, the internet made it trivially easy for people to just copy the articles’ content and share it beyond the paywall. The entire business model had collapsed, to the point that now only a select few major newspapers can even survive.That scale of copyright dilution and forced unbundling is the worst-case scenario for media businesses in the age of AI. It’s possible arts jobs could survive via consumers’ deep-seated aversion to explicitly AI-generated content, but AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer. Roughly 32% of workers in the overall arts, entertainment, and recreation sector use Generative AI to some extent, which is less than the 62% average across all industries, but still enough that virtually every major media project could have some AI within its workflow.Indeed, AI is likely seeping into media production processes in ways large companies themselves would struggle to prevent even when they desire to—how can a TV studio be sure nobody in their writers’ room is consulting ChatGPT for jokes or any storyboard artist is generating concept art? And even if professional TV and movie studios do effectively hold out against temptation and prevent internal AI use, how long can they compete with the large mass of wannabe independent creators with much fewer scruples? Plenty of media businesses tried to hold out against the algorithmic content waves of the 2010s and were buried as a result.Yet fundamentally, it’s difficult to meaningfully predict how new technologies will interact with existing arts businesses. Take the unexpected resurgence in book sales over the last four years. The novel as a commercial art form had been struggling for decades, with fewer books sold in 2019 than at the beginning of the millennium, but the last six years have seen an unprecedented 70% surge in sales. The unlikely savior of the printed word came from perhaps its polar opposite—TikTok.Of course, fewer people read now than ever before—for the general public, short-form video apps have accelerated the displacement of reading, just as TV, video games, or social media before them. Yet for a dwindling number of dedicated repeat readers, “BookTok” became a new way to source reviews, analysis, discourse, and community in a way that boosted the reading experience and absolutely turbocharged book sales. It’s possible that AI tools could have those same totally unpredictable spillovers for other museums, concerts, or other forms of art in ways that are unpredictable today, in much the same way short-form video saved books in ways that could never have been anticipated beforehand.At the end of the day, the arts are only a small sector of the overall macroeconomy. Media made up a small share of the labor market even at its peak, and it has always been difficult to get hired in creative industries to the point that making fun of art students’ job prospects became an easy punchline. The movie industry has an income profile closer to eggs or bicycles than something major like healthcare or finance. Were the goal to create art for art’s sake, for the intangible and nonmonetizable cultural benefits, it would be relatively easy to counterbalance any economic impacts of AI on artists just by reversing recent cuts to the National Endowments for the Arts & Humanities.It’s telling that Anthropic, the most prominent AI lab, has basically never bothered with image, video, or music generation, because the prospective economic benefits are marginal when compared to using AI to tackle math or scientific problems. OpenAI learned this lesson the hard way when it was forced to abandon its video generation platform Sora, deciding it had better use for its limited compute than making synthetic TikToks. Nowadays, the art generation is done primarily by secondary players running smaller models, though even these are large enough to threaten significant disruption to legacy media businesses.In other words, the primary impacts of AI art will be on culture and society rather than the macroeconomy. Yet arts jobs might be a microcosm for other “creative-adjacent” work that occupies a much larger share of economic activity. Take the tech sector itself, which is the clearest place where AI-driven job loss has shown up outside the media business, as powerful coding agents replace human programmers. Annual tech job gains stood at nearly 300k in 2022, but the sector has been bleeding jobs every year since then in what is now its longest labor market downturn.Right now, AI-driven job displacement has been relatively minor outside of these few narrow sectors. Unemployment is higher than it was four years ago but still below even the 2010s average, and overall job turnover rates remain extremely low. Some white-collar sectors that looked prime for AI automation have even been on a hiring spree over the last few years, including legal and engineering firms. Yet if the economic impact of AI ends up being anywhere near large enough to validate the trillions of dollars investors are currently betting on it, these economic disruptions will only spread from here.No posts

comments.author: jparishy
comments.textZhHtml:
I liked this article. I appreciate that it didn't try to say it is or isn't AI.

To me, the entertainment industry suffers from a lot of the same problems in most other industries that chase "efficiency", in terms of resources used and profit made. Economies and industries and labor are interdependent and more "alive" than balance sheets and bank accounts.

For the film industry, when you start moving things away from LA to "save money", it has knock on effects that happen over long periods of time. Multiple Quarterly Earnings Reports long, if you will. Local businesses that depend on the film industry close due to less work, so then there is less expertise available. Less expertise means it can command high prices. Suddenly it's too expensive to film in LA altogether. So the rest of the jobs leave too.

This pattern seems super common, not just in the film industry.

It is a narrative that interweaves with AI, too. AI is supposedly an efficiency boom. In the macroeconomy, who is the "efficiency" we are chasing for, who benefits? Who is getting the money that was "saved"? Regular people do not have more more money or time. The "efficiency" is for people who are already very rich, to get richer. Is that worth the price we're paying? I know my answer. The article gets close to it by mentioning the consolidation in Hollywood, but I do not see how we fix this without enforcing our antitrust laws. It is embarrassing what we let rich people do in the name of stock price go up.

comments.author: somenameforme
comments.textZhHtml:
In general I fully agree except with your conclusion. In the short-run efficiency immediately benefits the established players, but in the long-run it benefits, more or less literally, everybody except them. Because as you bring the price down on things you enable more efficient competition. Competition increases, margins decrease, baseline minimal standard of quality for success increases.

Software is a very clear example on this front. Valheim [1] is a game that was made mostly by one guy, at first at least. Not that long ago, this would have been a multi million dollar game produced by a wide array of people. It's just that tools, markets, and more have made it possible for even single developers to have an absurd degree of efficiency. And LLMs are probably going to bump this up exponentially.

This is why a metaphor I'm currently drawn to is one of people living in a very agrarian society just prior to the Industrial Revolution. What would they have envisioned being created? Super farms of course. And those super farms were indeed created, but the overall impact was such that those super farms became a practically inconsequential part of the overall economy. The future we're moving into isn't going to be the same but more efficient for those on top. That efficiency is going to revolutionize the economy in ways that are probably impossible to see from a distant, much how somebody living in an agrarian society couldn't have even begun to imagine the 'real' impact of the Industrial Revolution.

[1] - https://store.steampowered.com/app/892970/Valheim/

comments.author: bluegatty
comments.textZhHtml:
"that those super farms became a practically inconsequential part of the overall economy. " - not really.

Because farms are hyper competitive, it means that the surplus and efficiency gains are not kept by the farmers.

And it's not just 'super farms' - its' transportation that enabled 'regular labour farms' in low cost areas.

In this case, mostly to consumers.

You can see the charts for the kinds of work people used to do vs, now aka we used to all live on farms, now we do all sorts of things.

This is why we're seeing an pushback on globalization, economic optimization doesn't always balance out with strategic considerations aka food supply security etc. and those are hard to put on the books because they feel like a 'non-market force'.

A 'subsidy' feels like welfare, it's really and adjust of the balance of power.

comments.author: pembrook
comments.textZhHtml:
I'm amazed nobody has challenged OP on his narrative for why the film industry left LA since it's completely wrong.

It has nothing to do with 'evil corporations chasing efficiency.' And you rightly point out, efficiency/productivity is literally what raises living standards for everyone.

The truth is, rising living standards have increased leisure time globally, and increased leisure time leads to increased demand for entertainment fit to your culture.

China now has 2X as many movie theaters as the US does. India produces 2,500 films per year today vs. 500 in Hollywood. Ditto for Europe (2500 films produced last year). South Korea went from nothing to a global entertainment player in 10 years. Their industries are still smaller than Hollywood but growing at faster rates.

Just like what happened to Detroit in the 1970s when Auto manufacturers started having to compete with other countries who built domestic car industries, the same exact thing happened to Los Angeles.

In both 1970s Detroit and 2010s LA, companies had focused on monetizing old cash cows (the superhero film was the chevy land yacht) while the market evolved under their feet, and unions had inflated wages/costs to the point of being wildly uncompetitive, so the industry supply chain went global. LA also refused to allow building new homes, so talent couldn't afford to stay even at $1,000/day union rates just for holding a light (that's an actual union rate for a gaffer in LA).

We're still just at the beginning of this in entertainment.

Technology has enabled the production and distribution of high end video content to drop dramatically, while at the same time demand for entertainment shifted from being heavily western to being much more diverse.

comments.author: echelon
comments.textZhHtml:
This is exactly correct.

Overseas has so much film infrastructure now that Hollywood flies out the entire cast and essential crew (DP, etc.) to work on American productions overseas. They hire cheaper local crews (who are non-union), rent cheaper facilities, and even collect foreign tax subsidies.

It's far cheaper to produce everything in the UK, Eastern Europe, or Asia than it is to film in LA. Or even heavily tax-subsidized states like Georgia.

America can't compete on film production cost anymore. So it's halfway through the process of leaving, except for shots that need to film in iconic cities like New York for certain key scenes. But even then, you might see only part of the production happen in the US.

This started during the pandemic content streaming wars. There was a huge demand for content, American studios were shut down, and Amazon and Netflix dabbled with trying to shoot overseas. They found out the foreign infrastructure was just fine and that they just needed to teach the local crews a few things to be able to lift and shift the entire production pipeline. And it was so much cheaper that the choice to move everything was obvious.

comments.author: Kaedon
comments.textZhHtml: Overall feels right but started happening well before pandemic, back in 2012-2013, lots of shows in Romania, Atlanta, etc.

comments.author: pembrook
comments.textZhHtml:
Yea the pandemic is overfit as a reason for most things. Production had already left over the preceding decades.

Hollywood didn't lose its relevance overnight. It's been a slow moving process as the film -> digital -> portable transition made production cheaper, the internet made talent cultivation/distribution easier, studios and audiences expanded internationally, unions kept ratcheting up rates, LA refused to build homes while population ballooned, QE/ZIRP/0% rates re-inflated a housing bubble, unions kept raising rates to keep up with housing in LA, internet/social content began competing with studio productions hurting demand, the incestuous hollywood-to-traditional media marketing pipeline died (much of old print/tv media existed to market Hollywood stars and products), etc. etc.

There's a few billion people now who have TVs and enough leisure time to stream hours of film/tv content. This is just within the last 15 years.

comments.author: kmeisthax
comments.textZhHtml:
Funny you mention superhero films, because that's also what killed the American comic book industry.

If you go to a bookstore and ask someone not particularly familiar with the industry to go find a comic book; you are very likely to have them hand a manga or manhwa tankobon[0] back to you. Trade paperbacks[1] are sold in bookstores, but the western comics section will be a small fraction of the manga & manhwa section.

The root cause of this is that in the 80s, comic book companies - say it with me, folks! - underwent massive amounts of consolidation to chase efficiencies at the expense of their ability to innovate and their ability to withstand systemic shocks. The particularized version of this is that the comic book companies ceded their cultural ubiquity to milk comics fans dry.

The efficiency being chased was "direct sales" - i.e. selling comic books to dedicated comic book stores, rather than in mass-market areas like grocery stores. A key thing to note is that the mass-market sellers retain the right to return unsold inventory and get a refund[3], but comic book stores bought on "all sales final" terms. What this ultimately meant was that comic book publishers didn't have to worry about the quality of the books anymore.

There was a long-standing cultural stigma in the US that comic books are for children. This was itself downstream of a push to censor comics that was partially successful and resulted in the Comics Code stunting the growth of the medium[4] in the US. Eventually, thanks to - among other things, Marvel wanting to publish an anti-drug PSA in a Spiderman book - the Comics Code Authority lost their power and we were able to publish comic books for adults in the US again.

Anyway, Alan Moore wrote a really gritty Batman book and kicked off a rush to capitalize on a growing adult comics wave. This, along with a bunch of people realizing that old #1s of comics published during Baby Boomers' childhoods[5] were super rare kicked off a huge speculator wave. The comics publishers - who at this point were just DC and Marvel - saw the dollar signs and started flooding the market with slop to meet the demands of speculators who were buying #1s just because they were a #1.

This continued until it could not. In an act of supreme hubris, Marvel decided to buy a comics distributor in pursuit of extreme vertical integration and wound up completely destroying their ability to correctly print a book. Then they went bankrupt, got bought out by a corporate raider, and sold their movie rights to anyone who had a buck. DC wound up in the hands of WB (lol), Marvel became a Disney property.

Yes, the 2010s comic book movie wave was directly caused by the 1990s comic book industry's death. And, for that matter, the exact same extreme consolidation that killed comics is coming for Hollywood. Disney bought Fox, Larry Ellison bought Paramount and WB and merged them into Skydance. The entirety of America's cultural industries are looking more and more like DC and Marvel fighting over the ashes of a culturally dead country.

comments.author: pixelmonkey
comments.textZhHtml:
I was in the audience when you gave the 5-minute docker lightning talk at PyCon US Santa Clara in 2013. I remember chatting with a friend/colleague about it (https://nvie.com/about/) and we both agreed it was the most interesting lightning talk that day.

What’s funny, though, is that since it was “just” a lightning talk, it didn’t even make it into the roundup of notes I sent to my team after PyCon. But a mere year later, Docker was how my team (and seemingly everyone else) ran projects locally.

Any interesting memories from that day in 2013? From your perspective, what happened in the year that followed that caused docker to be adopted so widely? Were there other key moments or turning points?

comments.author: shykes
comments.textZhHtml:
> Any interesting memories from that day in 2013?

That day is forever engraved in my memory... Off the top of my head:

I signed up for a lightning talk expecting an audience of 10-20 people, for a confidential demo of our unfinished project that we had so far only showed in 1-1 demos. Imagine my surprise when I learned Pycon does lightning talks on the main stage!

The previous speaker didn't show, so I started early. In the recording you can hear me joke that perhaps I should get his time allocation too - the MC was not amused.

I went over time and had to speedtalk through the end.. The MC once again was not amused and practically shoved me off stage :-D

We had a small sponsor booth at the even, where our small marketing team was prepared to pitch our product (DotCloud) but was thoroughly confused when a horde of people showed up after the talk, to ask about "Docker" - which as far as they knew was the founder's side project.

I drove down to Santa Clara on my newly acquired motorcycle - my very first trip on the freeway. I remember telling myself, "today is the day to take all the risks!"
